1up: House music was born in Chicago in the early 1980s. The name is said to come from The Warehouse, the club where DJ Frankie Knuckles played.
Frankie Knuckles is often called the "Godfather of House".
The Roland TR-909 drum machine and TB-303 bass synth shaped house and acid house, even though neither sold well when they first came out.
Most house tracks sit between about 120 and 130 beats per minute, the speed of a brisk walk.
Techno grew up in Detroit at the same time house grew up in Chicago.
Kraftwerk's album Autobahn (1974) helped show that electronic music could be pop.
Deep house mixes house beats with jazzy chords and soft pads. Larry Heard's "Can You Feel It" (1986) is a classic of the sound.

cultureshock: Dub was born in Jamaica in the late 1960s, when engineers like King Tubby and Lee "Scratch" Perry stripped reggae down to drum and bass and added echo and reverb.
The "version" on the B-side of a Jamaican 7-inch single was often an instrumental, and it grew into dub.
Jamaican-born DJ Kool Herc brought sound system culture to the Bronx and helped start hip hop.
Reggae was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage in 2018.
Bob Marley and the Wailers' album Exodus was named album of the century by Time magazine in 1999.
The red, gold and green of Rastafari are tied to the Ethiopian flag.
Reggae's "skank" guitar chop lands on beats two and four of the bar.
vault: Hip hop is said to have begun at a back-to-school party in the Bronx on 11 August 1973, hosted by DJ Kool Herc.
"Boom bap" is the sound of the kick drum and the snare, and it names the classic 90s New York style.
The Amen break, a drum solo of about six seconds from a 1969 record, became one of the most sampled drum loops ever.
The Technics SL-1200 turntable launched in 1972 and became the standard DJ deck for decades.
The Sugarhill Gang's "Rapper's Delight" (1979) was one of the first rap singles to become a hit.
Digging in the crates, hunting through record stacks for rare breaks to sample, is a producer's rite of passage.
